'''Timothy''' ('''''Phleum pratense''''') is a species of [[perennial plant|perennial]] [[Poaceae|grass]] native to most of Europe and northern and western Asia.<ref name="PlantAtlas">{{cite web | title = Timothy ''Phleum pratense'' L. | website = PlantAtlas | url = https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.fwb | access-date = 2026-03-14 }}</ref><ref name="POWO"/> It is also known as '''timothy-grass''',  '''meadow cat's-tail''' or '''common cat's-tail'''.<ref>{{cite book|title=The Observer's Book of Grasses, Sedge and Rushes|author= Francis Rose |page= 112|year= 1976|isbn=0 7232 1533 2 |publisher= Frederick Warne and Co.}}</ref> It is a member of the genus ''[[Phleum]]'', which consists of 17 species of annual and perennial grasses.<ref name="POWOgenus">{{cite web | title = ''Phleum'' L. | website = Plants of the World Online | url = https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:18725-1 | access-date = 2026-03-14 }}</ref>

It is probably named after Timothy Hanson, a British farmer and [[agriculturalist]] said to have introduced it from [[New England]] to the [[Southern U.S.|southern United States]] in the early 18th century.<ref>{{cite news | date = 9 July 1859 | title = Timothy Grass | page = 4 | url = https://www.newspapers.com/clip/3258381/timothy_grass/ | access-date = 20 September 2015 | newspaper = The Louisville Daily Courier | via = [[Newspapers.com]] }} {{Open access}}</ref><ref>''Merriam-Webster's Collegiate Dictionary'', 11th ed., p. 1310.</ref><ref>''Oxford English Dictionary'', s.v. "timothy grass".</ref> Upon his recommendation it became a major source of [[hay]] and cattle fodder to British [[farmer]]s in the mid-18th century.<ref>''Reader's Digest Nature Lover's Library Wild Flowers of Britain'', p. 430, published 1988</ref>

Timothy has now become [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] throughout most of North America, eastern Asia, southern South America, and Australasia.<ref name="POWO"/>

==Description==
Timothy grows to {{cvt|150|cm|0}} tall, with [[leaf|leaves]] up to {{cvt|50|cm|0}} long and {{cvt|4|–|8|mm|1}} broad. The leaves are hairless, rolled rather than folded, and the lower sheaths turn dark brown.<ref name="Streeter">{{cite book | vauthors = Streeter D | date = 2010 | title = Flower Guide | publisher = Collins | pages = 632–633 | isbn = 978-0-00-718389-0 | publication-place = London }}</ref><ref name="Fitter">{{cite book | vauthors = Fitter RS, Fitter A | date = 1984 | title = Collins Guide to the Grasses, Sedges, Rushes, and Ferns of Britain and Northern Europe | publisher = Harpercollins Pub Limited | pages = 98–99 | isbn = 0-00-219136-9 | publication-place = London }}</ref>

It is a tufted grass, with no [[stolon]]s or [[rhizome]]s. The [[ligule]] is short and blunt.<ref name="Streeter"/>

The [[flower]]head is {{cvt|6|–|15|cm|0}} long (or more, in some [[cultivar]]s) and {{cvt|6|–|10|mm|1}} broad, with densely packed spikelets, the [[glume]]s with a 1–2 mm long awn. It flowers from June until August. The [[stamen]]s are purple.<ref name="Streeter"/><ref name="Fitter"/>

Timothy can be confused with [[Phleum bertolonii|smaller cat's-tail]] (''Phleum bertolonii''); this is most easily distinguished by its acute, not blunt, ligules.<ref name="PlantAtlas"/> [[Meadow foxtail]] (''Alopecurus pratensis'') or [[Phleum phleoides|purple-stem cat's-tail]] (''Phleum phleoides'') can also be confused.

It grows well in heavy soil, and is noted for its resistance to cold and drought, and thus ability to grow in dry upland or poor sandy soils. In [[pasture]] it tends to be overwhelmed by more competitive grasses. After cutting it grows slowly.

==Taxonomy==
Two [[subspecies]] have been distinguished by some authors, ''Phleum pratense'' subsp. ''pratense'', and ''Phleum pratense'' subsp. ''bertolonii'' on [[calcareous]] grassland;<ref name="Fitter"/><ref name="AusGrass2-subsp-pratense">{{cite web | date = 2010-07-06 | title = ''Phleum pratense'' subsp. ''pratense'' | website = AusGrass2 | url = http://ausgrass2.myspecies.info/content/phleum-pratense-subsp-pratense | access-date = 2021-06-12 }}</ref> however, the latter is now generally considered to be a separate species, smaller cat's-tail ''[[Phleum bertolonii]]'' DC.<ref name="POWO"/><ref name="POWO2">{{cite web | title = ''Phleum bertolonii'' DC. | website = Plants of the World Online | url = https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:415786-1 | access-date = 2026-03-14 }}</ref><ref name="PlantAtlas"/><ref name="PlantAtlas2">{{cite web | title = Smaller Cat's-tail ''Phleum bertolonii'' DC. | website = PlantAtlas | url = https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.fw8 | access-date = 2026-03-14 }}</ref><ref name="Streeter"/>

==Ecology==
[[File:Timothee (Phleum pratense subsp. pratense).jpg|thumb|upright|Inflorescence]]
Some [[caterpillar]]s use it as a food plant, e.g. the [[Essex skipper]] (''Thymelicus lineola'') and the [[Melanargia galathea|marbled white]] (''Melanargia galathea''). It also grows in roadsides and abandoned fields but generally requires nutrient-rich soils.

== Cultivation and uses ==
{{Unreferenced section|date=March 2026}}
It is commonly grown for [[cattle]] feed and, in particular, as [[hay]] for [[horse]]s. It is relatively high in fibre, especially when cut late. It is considered a harsh, coarse grass little relished by livestock if cut earlier. It is considered part of the standard mix for grass hay and provides quality [[equine nutrition|nutrition for horses]]. Timothy hay is a staple food for domestic pet [[rabbit]]s, [[guinea pig]]s, [[chinchillas]], and [[common degu|degu]]s, often making up the bulk of their diet. Timothy hay is rich in long fibres and its abrasive texture helps to grind down the teeth, keeping both the teeth and jaw in good order.

Plants persist through the winter. Dead, straw-coloured flowering stems may persist, but only for a short time, and can be recognised by the distinctive spike-like [[inflorescence]].

Timothy was unintentionally introduced to North America by early settlers, and was first described in 1711 by John Hurd from plants growing in [[New Hampshire]]. Hurd named the grass "hurd grass" but a farmer named Timothy Hanson began to promote cultivation of it as a hay about 1720, and the grass has been known by its present name since then.

=== Breeding objectives in timothy ===
{{Unreferenced section|date=March 2026}}
Breeding programs for forage grasses and especially timothy have been focusing on the improvement of dry matter yield, resistance to disease, dry matter digestibility, and nutritional value, which depends on target species and environment. Due to high phenotypic and genetic heterogeneity in individual plants, and the polyploidy of many species, breeding programmes for timothy are accompanied by some difficulties.{{cn|date=September 2023}}

==Confusion with other species==
It is often confused with [[Alopecurus pratensis|meadow foxtail]] (''Alopecurus pratensis''). Timothy flowers later, from June until August, whereas meadow foxtail flowers from April until June. The [[spikelet]]s of timothy are twin hornlike projections arranged in cylindrical [[panicle]]s, whereas foxtail has a soft, single [[awn (botany)|awn]].<ref>[http://www.bsbi.org.uk/identification.html bsbi.org.uk] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717004923/http://www.bsbi.org.uk/identification.html |date=2011-07-17 }}; description, retrieved 2010-12-1.</ref>

[[Phleum phleoides|Purple-stem cat's-tail]] (''Phleum phleoides'') prefers lighter soils and grows on [[chalk downland]].

[[Phalaris angusta|Timothy canary grass]] (''Phalaris angusta''), another species with a similar cylindrical panicle, is toxic to livestock.
